paras: The Central Park incident in Henderson, Kentucky, was a confrontation on a Sunday night in September 1903 in which a white man struck a Black woman and other whites then drove the Black people present out of the town's Central Park. The local Henderson Journal described it as "a small touch of race war fever," and the item was reprinted by the Louisville Courier-Journal and, with ironic comment, by the Salt Lake Herald.
Central Park, called by the Journal a "popular resort," was crowded that evening with "a large number of citizens, white and black," and nearly all its seats were taken.

According to the Henderson Journal, a Black woman made remarks "of somewhat insulting nature" toward or in the presence of a white woman, and the white woman's escort resented them. As the woman said "I'm as good as any white lady," the escort struck her. Other whites in the park then drove the remaining Black people out "in short order," after which, in the Journal's words, "peace soon settled upon the scene."
None of the reports names the woman, the escort or anyone else involved, and no report of an arrest or other official action appears in the coverage.

The only account is the Henderson Journal's, which survives in reprints and treated the episode as a brief disturbance that ended once the Black park-goers were gone. The Courier-Journal printed it on 18 September 1903 among miscellaneous items under the headline "Touce of Race War," without comment.

On 1 October the Salt Lake Herald quoted the item in full in an editorial titled "A Kentucky Solution," offering it to "the race problem theorists" with the remark "Thus decently and in order was the thing done." The Herald mocked the idea that a Black woman's claim to be as good as a white woman was a "casus belli" and noted there was no evidence of hostilities "aside from the smacking administered to the colored lady." It closed by contrasting Kentucky with Indiana, Illinois and other Northern states, where it said Black people were "hanged and shot, sometimes burned at stakes," whereas in Kentucky "they are merely pushed out and away."
No coverage of the incident was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Central Park incident in Henderson, Kentucky
bases: After one Black woman was struck, whites drove the other Black people out of a public park without reported further injury, a forced removal from a public space rather than a lasting expulsion from the town (A1, A2).
Both surviving reports reprint the same Henderson Journal item verbatim, so the event rests on one local white source (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Henderson Journal (local white paper), as reprinted
accounts.gist: A Black woman's 'somewhat insulting' remarks were resented by a white lady's escort, who struck her; other whites drove the Black people from the park and 'peace soon settled upon the scene.'

accounts.label: Salt Lake Herald editorial
accounts.gist: Took the Journal's account at its word but mocked the pretext, saying there was no evidence of hostilities beyond the blow and that in Kentucky Black people were 'merely pushed out and away.'

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal ran the Henderson Journal item unchanged under the headline 'Touce of Race War', amid miscellany, with no comment.
The Salt Lake Herald's 'A Kentucky Solution' ridiculed the idea that the woman's words were a 'casus belli' but praised Kentucky's method as better than lynchings in Indiana and Illinois.

record_check.record: After a Black woman's remark to a white lady at Central Park, whites in Henderson, Ky., drove other Black people out of the park on a Sunday night in September 1903.
record_check.dossier: Correct, but it omits that the white lady's escort struck the woman before the others were driven out.
An unnamed Black woman (struck) and other unnamed Black park-goers (driven out).
One woman struck; no other injuries reported.
Remarks 'of somewhat insulting nature' to or near a white lady ('I'm as good as any white lady'), a racial-offense pretext.
The white lady's escort and other whites in the park.
A Sunday night before 18 September 1903; the exact date is not given.
Single source: one Henderson Journal item, reprinted twice.

sources.note: Reprints the Henderson Journal item 'Touce [Touch] of Race War': a white man struck a Black woman at Central Park on a Sunday night and whites drove Black people from the park.
quotes: Henderson had a small touch of race war fever at Central Park Sunday night.
Other whites in the park took up the fever and proceeded to drive other negroes from the park, which they did in short order, and peace soon settled upon the scene.
